name: Karl Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Karl, thanks for talking with me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential. To start, what kind of line work do you do?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior on a transmission crew for the big regional grid company, so the tall steel towers, not the street poles. A lot of it is building new lines out to wind farms, and when there's a big storm they send us all over to restore power. I've been at it about eighteen months.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: If we're on a build, I'm up at five in a motel somewhere, we drive out to the site and do the safety briefing in the mud. My job right now is mostly rigging, bolting tower sections on the ground, running the winch, helping string the conductor. The view from the towers is amazing when they let me go up, and the guys are good, especially Bjørn, who's been teaching me for a year. What wears me out is the travel; I'm away from Mia maybe two weeks a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I mostly say now, which is that the grid needs more people, not fewer. Every country is trying to electrify everything, and someone has to build the lines. I'd probably add that AI is good for writing emails and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it's good news. The demand for transmission work is huge and it's not slowing down, so I'd have work for life. I'd get my full ticket, maybe go for crew leader one day, and Mia and I would buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I'd keep putting the overtime money into the house deposit, we're at about forty percent of it. I'd keep using the AI chat thing now and then to check a rule in the safety manual, because it's quicker than the binder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change about the travel in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, sadly. The wind farms are where they are. I'd probably try for a role on the maintenance side in a few years so I'm home more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the crew who'd still have a hard time, even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bjørn's knees, honestly. He's 55 and climbing every day. That's not an AI problem, that's a pension and health problem, and I think the company should be doing more about it.

S0.say: Karl would say the grid needs more workers, not fewer, because electrification means someone has to build the lines. He'd add that AI is good for writing emails and little else.
S0.think: Privately he sees this as good news, with transmission work in strong demand for decades. He expects to finish his ticket, aim for crew leader and buy a house with his partner.
S0.do: Keeps working and keeps putting overtime pay into the house deposit, which is about forty percent saved. Continues using an AI chat tool occasionally to look up safety rules.
S0.feel: Calm and fairly happy about the future.
S0.quote: That's not an AI problem, that's a pension and health problem, and I think the company should be doing more about it.
S0.fieldNote: Karl's sense of security comes from the energy transition, not from savings alone. His first concern in a calm world was his mentor's knees, which shows where his progressive instincts sit. He already uses AI for small things without any fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers should share in the time it saves. If an AI does the paperwork and the planning, give us a shorter week, don't cut the crew. I'd say that in the union meeting and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly fine for me. Planning, inspections, drones flying the lines looking for damage, sure. But bolting a tower in the wind is still a person for a while yet. The office staff in planning are the ones who'd take the hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw the drone inspections really working, I'd want to learn to fly them, because that's a skill that travels with you. I'd ask the company if they'd pay for the drone licence, it's about a week's course. And I'd stay in the union, maybe go to more meetings than I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little restless, but okay. It's more interesting than scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn drones once they were working. Why not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the company buy stuff that ends up in a shed. Two years ago they bought these fancy laser rangefinders and nobody uses them. I'll jump when the other crews have jumped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you know in planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linnea, who sorts our crew schedules. She's great, she knows which motels have hot water. If an AI takes over that job, I hope she gets moved somewhere decent, but I wouldn't bet on it.

S1.say: Karl would argue in the union and online that workers should share in time saved by AI, through a shorter week rather than smaller crews.
S1.think: Privately he thinks his own hands-on work is fine for a while, with AI taking planning and inspections. He expects office staff in planning to be hit first.
S1.do: Plans to train as a drone pilot once he sees drone inspections working on other crews, asking the company to pay for the week-long licence course. Goes to more union meetings.
S1.feel: A little restless but more interested than scared.
S1.quote: Two years ago they bought these fancy laser rangefinders and nobody uses them. I'll jump when the other crews have jumped.
S1.fieldNote: Karl shows his steady adaptability clearly: willing to change, but only after seeing proof on other crews. His public line is about sharing gains, while privately he feels largely safe. His concern for the scheduler Linnea was specific and warm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a public emergency and the government has to step in, with guaranteed income and the grid kept in public hands. I'd be at protests, probably. Mia's union would be out too, because teachers would be in it just as bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the towers would last a bit longer than people expect, because the sites are muddy and wild and every one is different. But two years? I'm not good enough yet to be the person they keep. They'd keep Bjørn to supervise the robots, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop taking the long-distance jobs if I could and stay closer to home, because if it's all going to change I want to be near Mia. We'd hold off on buying the house, which kills me, but you don't sign a mortgage when you don't know what work there'll be. I'd keep the deposit money in the bank as our cushion and join whatever action the union organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight-chest kind of feeling, especially about the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what happens to the house plan, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes in the drawer. We've been looking at a little place on the edge of Mia's town with a garden, and I'd ring the agent and say not yet. That deposit becomes our life raft instead of our front door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's an emergency, but you also think the towers would last longer than people expect. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. For me the towers might last a bit. For the country, two years is an emergency, because everyone gets hit at once and nobody's ready.

S2.say: Karl would call it a public emergency and demand government action: a guaranteed income and the grid kept in public hands. He'd expect to protest alongside his partner's teachers' union.
S2.think: Privately he thinks tower work may last longer than expected because each site is different. But as a junior he doubts he'd be the one kept to supervise robots.
S2.do: Asks to stop long-distance jobs to stay near his partner, and shelves the house purchase, keeping the deposit as a cushion. Joins union protests calling for an income guarantee.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest, mostly about the house.
S2.quote: That deposit becomes our life raft instead of our front door.
S2.fieldNote: The fastest scenario changes Karl's biggest life decision rather than his job hunting. He's clear-eyed that seniority, not skill alone, decides who stays. He handled the contradiction well by separating his own case from the country's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if the government actually plans. I'd push the union to get retraining money into the next contract. I'd say it calmly, though, because I think panic helps the bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to finish my ticket and get good. And good lineworkers who also understand the machines will be the ones running the robot crews. I think I could be one of them if I move at the right time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around year two, once I saw the first robot crews on other jobs, I'd get on whatever training the company offered, drones first, then robot operation. We'd probably still buy the house, but a cheaper one, so the mortgage could be paid on Mia's wage alone. And I'd talk to Bjørn about which skills he thinks will outlast the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's also a bit of excitement in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you work out that it should be a house Mia's wage can cover alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We sat down once with a spreadsheet when I first started, just for fun, and worked out what we could do on one wage. It's about two-thirds of what we were looking at. Five years gives us time to save the difference, which two years doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone just starting their apprenticeship now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say still do it, but learn the computer side too. Like I said with the steady one, the people who understand both will be fine. The people who only know one side, I'm not sure.

S3.say: Karl would say five years is enough if the government actually plans, and push the union to win retraining money in the next contract. He'd stay calm in public, believing panic helps employers.
S3.think: Privately he believes five years is enough to finish his ticket and become skilled. He thinks lineworkers who understand the machines will run the robot crews, and he could be one.
S3.do: Signs up for drone and robot-operation training around year two, once robot crews appear on other jobs. Buys a cheaper house that his partner's wage could cover alone, and asks his mentor which skills will last.
S3.feel: Uneasy with a thread of excitement.
S3.quote: We sat down once with a spreadsheet when I first started, just for fun, and worked out what we could do on one wage.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips Karl from defence to a plan: the house survives, scaled down, and he times his retraining for when others have proven it. He thinks in terms of a household of two, not just himself. His caution and his progressive politics sit side by side easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it arguing. I'd want a national plan for grid workers, with the unions writing half of it. Online I'd probably share stories of people who'd made the jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. I'd be 37 with years on the towers, and I'd have time to move into whatever the job becomes. My worry is more about everyone else, like the guys who are 50 now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing dramatic. We'd buy the house, I'd finish my apprenticeship, and I'd keep an eye on which crews get the robots first. I'd probably do a short course on the AI planning tools the company uses, once a couple of the other juniors had tried it and said it was worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit of worry in the back of my head, but nothing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the guys who are 50 now. What happens to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years they're 60, so maybe they make it to retirement just as it lands. Bjørn would be 65, so he'd squeak through. It's the 45-year-olds I worry about, too young to stop, too old to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change anything about having a family someday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, we've talked about it. With ten years I think we'd go ahead with kids in a few years. With two, I'm not sure we would, not with nothing certain.

S4.say: Karl would call ten years a gift and push for a national plan for grid workers co-written by unions. He'd share stories of people who'd successfully changed roles.
S4.think: Privately he thinks he'd be fine, aged 37 with years of tower experience and time to shift into the new version of the job. His worry is for workers in their mid-40s.
S4.do: Buys the house and finishes his apprenticeship in the first year. Takes a short course on the company's AI planning tools once other juniors recommend it.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a little worry at the back of his mind.
S4.quote: It's the 45-year-olds I worry about, too young to stop, too old to start over.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture restores almost all of Karl's plans, including children. His worry shifts outward to colleagues in mid-career, which fits his union outlook. The contrast with the two-year picture shows how much the timeline drives his family decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it hits me and Mia at the same time and we'd have to freeze everything. What would help is a guaranteed income for a while, and the grid staying public so the savings go back to people, not shareholders.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like for partners. Everyone asks the worker, but Mia's the one who'd be doing the maths at the kitchen table with me. Her job's on the line in those pictures too.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks the worker, but Mia's the one who'd be doing the maths at the kitchen table with me.
portrait: Karl Jensen is a 27-year-old junior on a transmission crew building towers out to wind farms, away from home about two weeks a month. He's saving hard for a house with his partner Mia, a teacher, and already uses AI chat tools for small jobs. He changes only once he's seen something work on other crews, and his politics lean toward unions and public ownership. He's calm in the slower pictures, anxious when AGI comes in two years and freezes his house plans, and calm again with ten years to prepare.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would hit both him and his partner at once and force them to freeze their plans.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for a time, and keeping the grid public so the gains go to people rather than shareholders.
